atlas.title: A debt, written in clay
atlas.body: An Old Assyrian tablet from Anatolia records silver owed to a merchant, staged repayment and witnesses. The object puts writing and enforceable promises at the center of monetary history. Coins are not required for a sophisticated loan.
atlas.prompt: Read the terms: who owes whom, in what unit, and when?
atlas.imageAlt: Clay tablet covered in closely spaced cuneiform impressions; a surviving record of a silver loan.
atlas.imageCredit: The Met · 66.245.17a · Klejman gift, 1966 · Public Domain

atlas.title: A thousand cash on paper
atlas.body: The Met’s Ming-period yi guan is ink on mulberry-bark paper. Its stated denomination translates a count of cash into a portable printed object. A denomination is a claim; it does not by itself establish purchasing power.
atlas.prompt: Compare the physical size and material with a modern note.

atlas.title: A record of relationships
atlas.body: Onondaga describes wampum as a vital Haudenosaunee cultural practice. Shell beads and belts carry commitments and histories. Reducing these objects to a primitive form of cash removes the social and political relationships they record.
atlas.prompt: Use community-authored accounts before assigning an economic category.

atlas.title: Silver and its human cost
atlas.body: Potosí connects the material history of money to colonial extraction. UNESCO’s account includes the mining infrastructure and forced Indigenous labor. Study the people and landscape behind precious metal, alongside the objects minted from it.
atlas.prompt: Map the route from a mine to a monetary object. Who bears the cost?

atlas.title: Money as a bank liability
atlas.body: The Bank of England explains that commercial-bank lending creates deposits. A bank balance is a claim on an institution, rather than a box of banknotes assigned to one customer. Lending is constrained by policy, risk and the bank’s balance sheet.
atlas.prompt: Draw the loan and matching deposit on two balance sheets.

atlas.title: Acceptance is contextual
atlas.body: Legal tender has a narrow debt-settlement meaning in the UK. The term does not require every shop to accept every note. Monetary acceptance, contract terms and legal-tender status are related questions with different answers.
atlas.prompt: Separate a shop’s acceptance policy from settlement of a debt.

atlas.title: A rail is not a currency
atlas.body: Brazil’s Pix is an instant-payment arrangement. Moving a balance quickly is different from creating a new unit of account. Interface, directory, settlement and underlying money belong in separate parts of a system diagram.
atlas.prompt: Draw what changes and what stays in reais when a payment moves.

atlas.title: An agreement about a ledger
atlas.body: NIST describes distributed ledgers and mechanisms for agreeing on their contents. A blockchain can record tokens and transfers, but the meaning and rights of an entry depend on its application. Technical immutability does not settle every off-chain dispute.
atlas.prompt: Identify the validators, upgrade authority and failure recovery.

atlas.title: A peg is a design problem
atlas.body: The BIS examines stablecoins through monetary-system criteria including singleness, elasticity and integrity. Studying a stablecoin requires inspecting reserves, redemption terms, issuer and operating network; its name is not evidence of guaranteed value.
atlas.prompt: Compare holder rights with commercial-bank deposits.

atlas.title: Whose liability is digital money?
atlas.body: The Federal Reserve describes a CBDC as a digital form of central-bank money. This is a definition, not a claim that a particular proposed public system is operating. Design choices include intermediaries, privacy, resilience and access.
atlas.prompt: List the choices a pilot must resolve before a launch.

atlas.title: A token and the rights around it
atlas.body: The US Copyright Office and USPTO examine the gap between token ownership and intellectual-property rights. An edition record should say which physical item, file and license are included. A token alone does not automatically transfer copyright.
atlas.prompt: Write separate clauses for object ownership and reproduction rights.

atlas.title: A note that represents a place
atlas.body: An original art note can use numbering, narrative and print craft without promising redemption. This proposal treats the artifact as a collectible, with a visible creator record and no monetary value. No physical samples have been approved.
atlas.prompt: Design a civic story; document whose permission is needed.

atlas.title: A shell within a trade network
atlas.body: Cowries were monetary objects in several regions, as well as adornments and cultural objects. The Smithsonian’s account connects their African trade history to power and enslavement. Avoid treating a material’s portability as a complete explanation of its social role.
atlas.prompt: Track supply and exchange power alongside the shell itself.

atlas.title: Value without moving the stone
atlas.body: The Smithsonian’s forms-of-money exhibition includes a Yapese stone ring. Rai invites inquiry into remembered ownership and the story of an object’s acquisition. This museum object’s date is not the origin date of the tradition.
atlas.prompt: What must a community know for a stationary object to retain value?

atlas.title: A lion stamped in electrum
atlas.body: The British Museum catalogs a Lydian third-stater made from electrum, weighing 4.67 g and measuring up to 13 mm. Its lion and incuse marks invite questions about issuing authority and recognition. It is an early coin example, not a claim to the first money.
atlas.prompt: Compare what a mark tells a user with what must be measured.

atlas.title: Many marks, many authorities
atlas.body: The RBI Museum presents silver punch-marked coinage among ancient Indian monetary forms. Individually punched symbols differ from cast shapes and later portrait coins. Regional chronology varies; a single date would flatten those differences.
atlas.prompt: Why does a coin need neither a round outline nor a ruler’s portrait?

atlas.title: A tool shape becomes a sign
atlas.body: The British Museum’s Qi bronze knife-money example is approximately 186 mm long. Its form opens a question about monetary recognition: an object can keep a familiar shape while acquiring a different use within exchange.
atlas.prompt: Distinguish evidence of shape from claims about actual tool use.

atlas.title: Words travel with a coin
atlas.body: The Met’s Syrian gold dinar bears inscriptions following Abd al-Malik’s late-seventh-century monetary reform. Its textual design shows that repeated public messages need not be portraits. The date and collection identity are documented; interpretation should remain source-linked.
atlas.prompt: Annotate authority, lettering and material without inventing a reading.
atlas.imageAlt: Gold dinar with Arabic inscriptions, dated 79 AH, corresponding to 698–99 CE.
atlas.imageCredit: The Met · 99.35.2386 · Durkee bequest, 1898 · Public Domain

atlas.title: A promise with withdrawals
atlas.body: The Bank of England Museum documents an early running-cash-note fragment recording a £22 deposit withdrawn in two payments. It brings a paper promise and the underlying account into the same story. Its function differs from the Ming paper object.
atlas.prompt: Where does a receipt end and transferable money begin?

atlas.title: A local promise on a clamshell
atlas.body: The Smithsonian catalogs a one-dollar Pismo Beach clamshell made by Restwell Cabins. It offers a California case of improvised local money in 1933. Appearance and denomination alone do not tell us the full redemption or acceptance arrangements.
atlas.prompt: What evidence would establish who accepted it and on what terms?

atlas.title: Emergency money meets collecting
atlas.body: The British Museum’s exhibition examines German emergency money over the First World War and its aftermath. Emergency use and collecting appeal are distinct roles; an issue’s design, date and use need to be checked individually.
atlas.prompt: Can collector demand change what an issuer makes?

atlas.title: A prepaid service, then a collectible
atlas.body: The Penny Black prepaid postage. Its later value to collectors is a different question from the postal service represented by its original face value. Keep service entitlement, physical artifact and collector asking price in separate catalog fields.
atlas.prompt: How is prepaid postage different from general-purpose money?

atlas.title: A stamp gains a protective case
atlas.body: During the U.S. Civil War coin shortage, encased postage protected stamps used as small-payment substitutes. Gault’s cases also carried advertising. The monetary role came from particular circumstances, not a timeless identity of all postage stamps.
atlas.prompt: Can packaging change how an object circulates?

atlas.title: An account unit at the trading post
atlas.body: The Bank of Canada Museum describes the made-beaver unit in fur-trade exchange. A company’s account unit and exchange terms affected the relationships between traders and Indigenous communities. Record power and negotiated terms alongside the token or tally.
atlas.prompt: Who determines a unit’s exchange terms, and who can challenge them?

vendors.name: Lanklu Designs
vendors.body: Default U.S.-size, visible-fiber cotton-linen, no enhancements; $1.56 per note before shipping and tax. Sequential numbering available and included. A 150 × 75 mm custom size needs its own quote. Laser printing; physical quality untested.

vendors.name: CatPrint
vendors.body: Parent research recorded $16.35 for 3 duplex pieces and $18.35 for 15 unique duplex pieces: 150 × 75 mm (rounded inches), 80 lb text Medium Letter Plain, full color/full bleed, quantity one per design, no finishing; before shipping/tax. Recreate all settings before relying on it.

vendors.name: Etched in Ashes
vendors.body: 40 mm, double-sided brass laser engraving, before shipping and tax. A prototype route; engraving is not die striking. No physical inspection or commissioned proof has occurred.

vendors.name: Custom Challenge Coins
vendors.body: 1.5-inch no-color benchmark: 25 × $9.18 plus $100 mold. Standard shipping advertised as included; confirm upgrades/tax and quote applicability. Manufacturing and delivery remain unconfirmed for our design.

vendors.name: MyEventNote / Enschedé
vendors.body: Vendor describes cotton material, offset, intaglio and numbering. Price and minimum run remain unresolved. Capabilities are vendor claims, not an inspected specimen.

modules.title: Reading an object
modules.body: Inspect an object’s material, marks, issuer and denomination. Distinguish catalog facts from what you infer.
modules.activity: Produce a 150-word label with a source, date, uncertainty and rights note.
modules.check: A label is successful when another reader can verify each factual claim.

modules.title: Credit before the coin
modules.body: Read the Old Assyrian loan tablet. Compare a written obligation with a transferable object; neither is a complete account of all early monetary systems.
modules.activity: Diagram borrower, lender, witnesses, unit and repayment schedule.
modules.check: Check: is the tablet evidence of a promise or the silver itself?

modules.title: Money and cultural authority
modules.body: Read Onondaga’s explanation of wampum. Notice how ceremonial and political meaning differs from an outsider’s cash classification.
modules.activity: Write two labels: one reductive, one grounded in the community’s account.
modules.check: Explain which relationships the second label preserves.

modules.title: Printing a promise
modules.body: Examine the Ming paper object and its denomination. Paper’s lightness and reproducibility raise questions about issuer credibility and control.
modules.activity: Compare material, face value and observed market price as distinct fields.
modules.check: A high printed number is not evidence of high purchasing power.

modules.title: The material supply chain
modules.body: Connect silver to mining infrastructure and labor at Potosí. A beautiful monetary object can carry a violent production history.
modules.activity: Create a four-stage supply-chain map with one missing-evidence question.
modules.check: Include people and environmental costs, not just shipping routes.

modules.title: Where deposits come from
modules.body: Study the Bank of England’s lending explanation. Add a loan asset and a matching deposit liability; then model repayment.
modules.activity: Make a balance-sheet worksheet for a hypothetical loan.
modules.check: Do assets and liabilities still reconcile? No real money is issued.

modules.title: Payment rails
modules.body: Compare Pix with a new currency. A rail can change transfer speed without changing the unit of account.
modules.activity: Draw initiation, messaging, settlement and confirmation separately.
modules.check: Name the underlying balance rather than calling every app a currency.

modules.title: Ledger governance
modules.body: Use NIST’s overview to distinguish permissioned and permissionless systems. Trace validation, key loss, upgrades and dispute handling.
modules.activity: Prepare a system card with five governance questions.
modules.check: Consensus records agreement; it does not eliminate governance.

modules.title: Future-of-money seminar
modules.body: Read the BIS proposal alongside the CBDC explainer. Treat proposed architectures as hypotheses. Separate technical capacity from political adoption.
modules.activity: Compare three scenarios using privacy, resilience, access and holder rights.
modules.check: What evidence would change your preference?

modules.title: Print preflight lab
modules.body: Use the original-art note template. Confirm trim, bleed, safe area, fonts, raster resolution and front/back orientation.
modules.activity: Produce a marked proof and a physical-sample checklist.
modules.check: Screen color is not a contract for the printed result.

modules.title: Collecting and provenance
modules.body: Write a record for an art note: creator, edition, material, serial range, file version, rights and replacement policy.
modules.activity: Separate the object, downloadable file and copyright license.
modules.check: What can the owner reproduce, and what must remain credited?

modules.title: Print shop economics
modules.body: Adjust the batch model below. Test sell-through before buying equipment; unsold stock still consumes cash.
modules.activity: Compare 15 and 25 sets sold, then double labor cost.
modules.check: Explain why markup per note differs from cash left after a batch.

roles.title: Currency research editor
roles.deliverable: Maintain object labels, date ranges and primary-source bibliography; deliver five reviewed case additions.
roles.supervision: Editorial mentor approval before any publication.

roles.title: Print resource librarian
roles.deliverable: Version templates and vendor requirements; deliver a dated comparison and reusable preflight sheet.
roles.supervision: Production mentor verifies each technical claim.

roles.title: Specimen lab assistant
roles.deliverable: Photograph authorized samples and record trim, registration, line detail and paper behavior.
roles.supervision: A production mentor controls sample ordering and quality sign-off.

roles.title: Edition provenance researcher
roles.deliverable: Prototype serial registers, artist credits, license fields and replacement records.
roles.supervision: Rights and edition policies approved by project lead.

roles.title: Access and learning tester
roles.deliverable: Test mobile navigation, keyboard controls and UES exercises; deliver reproducible issues.
roles.supervision: Learning mentor reviews exercises and accessibility findings.

roles.title: Print economics analyst
roles.deliverable: Compare sell-through, fulfillment time and packaging with approved cost data.
roles.supervision: Business mentor owns assumptions and commercial decisions.
